question.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits,  as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5}{2(x-2)^{8}} & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can sketch the graph of $y=\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}$ as follows:

1\. Take the graph of $y=\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}.$

2\. Translate it to the right by $2$ units. This gives $y=\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273867/assets/81491bb2e7201fd249d6c3ac3a7ec1d902f612887cb59a5155b60308f42e2f8f.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to ({2}^{-})}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}=\infty ,\,{lim}_{x\to ({2}^{+})}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}=\infty ,
$$

and therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}=\infty .
$$

The positive factor of $\frac{5}{2}$ does not change the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{5}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{8}}=\infty .
$$
